episodes.title: Gold’s rollercoaster ride
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
HSBC's precious metals analyst Jim Steele reviews gold's volatile 2026 round trip — an all-time high above $5,400/oz in February followed by a sharp selloff below $4,000 — and frames the drivers shaping the metal's next moves, with direct read-through for the dollar and global risk appetite that EM traders track closely.

**Key points**
- Gold hit a record above $5,400 in February before falling sharply, in the most volatile 12-month stretch of Steele's career.
- Central banks bought roughly one in every three ounces mined in 2022-24; ECB research showed gold reserves surpassed US Treasury holdings in value for the first time in modern finance.
- The rally was also fueled by expectations of 50-60bp of Fed cuts, dollar weakness and lower real yields; FOMO drove new retail/speculative entrants, especially from August last year.
- Gold broke its traditional safe-haven pattern around the Iran strike, selling off instead of rallying as an oil-driven inflation scare pushed yields and the dollar higher, triggering liquidation by new entrants and portfolio hedgers.
- Sanctions use has reinvigorated central-bank gold demand as a hedge against being frozen out of dollar assets (per economist Barry Eichengreen); central banks are less price-sensitive but still reducing purchase pace off highs.
- Gold tokenization/ETFs are broadening the investor base toward smaller, lower-income-country buyers, notably India.

**FX / rates implications**
- Gold retains an inverse relationship with the dollar/DXY except in acute crisis episodes (COVID, GFC) when both rise together — a strong dollar remains a headwind for gold and, by extension, a broader EM FX headwind.
- A shift in Fed rate-cut expectations toward neutral would weaken the dollar and be gold-positive, a tailwind that would also ease funding costs and support EM Asia/LATAM carry trades.
- Rising US fiscal deficits and debt issuance are flagged as structurally gold-supportive, a theme relevant to UST 10y term premium and broader EM risk sentiment.

**Watch list**
- Dollar/DXY direction and evolving Fed rate-cut expectations under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
- US fiscal deficit trajectory and potential flashpoints around the US midterm elections.
- Pace of central-bank gold buying and any further sanctions-driven reserve diversification.

episodes.title: Ep. 375: Bilal on How to Use AI to Turbocharge Your Market Analysis
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Bilal Hafeez, Head of Strategy at Macro Hive, departs from market commentary to explain his personal workflow for using AI/LLMs to accelerate financial research and market analysis. The episode is a how-to on AI tooling rather than a discussion of any specific market, currency, or macro driver, so direct trading relevance is minimal, though the framework may be of interest to analysts looking to streamline their own research process.

**Key points**
- Six themes covered: LLMs democratizing coding (natural language to Python/code), structured prompting via a "CLEAR" framework (Context, Length/format, Examples, Ask it to think, Role/persona), building reusable "skills" (e.g. an article-summarizer skill, a Tufte-style chart-formatting skill), customizing AI memory across sessions, using continuous/agentic work (Claude's "co-work", ChatGPT's "work") to run scheduled tasks like daily academic-paper digests, and building a personal RAG/knowledge base from trusted sources (IMF, BIS, central banks, followed newsletters/Twitter accounts).
- Emphasizes evaluating prompts against a self-produced "gold standard" output before trusting LLM output.
- Notes RAG systems reduce hallucination, provide source audit trails, and can be time-filtered (e.g., only documents from the past 24 hours) to stay current with fast-moving markets.
- Mentions Macro Hive's acquisition by BGC Group and the launch of Macro Hive Markets, a new execution-services offering alongside strategy/quant research.

**FX / rates implications**
None directly — no currencies, rates, central bank policy, or specific market catalysts are discussed in this episode.

**Watch list**
- None specific; episode is a productivity/methodology piece rather than a market-moving update.

episodes.title: Strategic Stalemate: Ryan Hass on How Beijing Sees America — and Trump
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Brookings China Center director Ryan Hass discusses two essays on China's evolving worldview: a China Leadership Monitor piece arguing Beijing has moved from participant to architect of an alternative international political order, and a Brookings piece on why Xi Jinping is not effusively embracing Trump's conciliatory posture ahead of a planned September state visit to Washington. This is a geopolitical/foreign-policy deep dive with limited direct FX/rates trading signal, but it frames the US-China strategic backdrop that periodically drives risk sentiment and CNY positioning.

**Key points**
- Hass argues China increasingly sees itself in "strategic stalemate" with the US, citing the 2025 trade war where US tariffs on China hit 145% before Trump backed down.
- China's foreign aid remains flat near $4bn vs US at roughly $50bn even after cuts, and BRI policy-bank lending has shrunk, showing a gap between rhetorical ambition and resource commitment.
- Neither US nor China currently has "economic escalation dominance" (ability to inflict pain the other can't replicate/absorb), per Dalip Singh framework — rare earths (China) vs chips/jet engines (US) are the key leverage points.
- A US-China trade truce reached in Busan a year ago expires in November; some tariff exemptions and Chinese purchases of US goods are expected at the upcoming summit, alongside an AI risk-reduction dialogue with low expectations for major breakthroughs.
- Japan and Philippines are raising defense budgets and deepening US coordination in response to Chinese pressure in the East/South China Seas and around Taiwan.

**FX / rates implications**
- Limited direct read-through for EM FX/rates, but the November expiry of the US-China trade truce and any signs of tariff re-escalation are a tail-risk catalyst for CNY/CNH and broader EM Asia risk sentiment (KRW, TWD, THB exposed via China trade linkages).
- A stable-to-cooling US-China relationship (as Hass expects, contrarian to Washington consensus) would be modestly supportive of global risk appetite and EM carry trades broadly.
- Ongoing Japan/Philippines-China tensions are a slow-burn geopolitical risk factor for regional risk premia but not an immediate market mover.

**Watch list**
- Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington later in September 2026.
- US-China trade truce expiration in November 2026 — watch for tariff snapback risk.
- Pre-summit US-China AI dialogue outcome.
- 21st Party Congress next fall (leadership succession signals under Xi's potential fourth term).

episodes.title: Through the Noise: Inching towards a Fed ‘credibility’ hike
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This episode covers a heavy global central-bank week — a near-certain Fed hike, an ECB hike just delivered, and an upcoming BoJ decision — plus an oil price risk near $100/bbl, all of which drive the dollar, UST yields and DM FX crosses that set the tone for EM positioning.

**Key points**
- Fed: August payrolls added 162,000 jobs (nearly triple consensus), unemployment held at 4.1% (full employment), but wage growth slowed to a five-year low of 3.1% y/y; producer price inflation accelerated in August, making a 25bp Fed hike next week highly likely absent a soft CPI print.
- Fed Chair Wash called the current 3.75% policy rate "not restrictive"; a hold amid perceived Trump administration pressure could undermine Fed credibility and weigh on equities/bonds.
- ECB hiked 25bp to 2.5%, citing Middle East conflict/energy shock inflation pressure; Lagarde called it a "no-brainer"; strategists expect another 25bp hike by December, deposit rate potentially reaching 2.75%.
- US 10y yield faces major resistance near 5.02% (2023 high); CTA/managed futures shorts at record levels; house raised bond maturity preference to 3-7 years from 3-5 years, favoring corporates over governments.
- Oil near $100/bbl on Gulf export disruption risk, Iran tanker actions, and China resuming buying; US crude inventories below 5-year range; house hedges oil upside via US inflation-protected bonds rather than equities.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed hike would support USD broadly and cap EUR/GBP/JPY gains, with DXY seen holding near 99.8-100 — a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades.
- EUR/USD sees gradual upside toward 1.18 resistance, but a Fed hike could delay the break higher; USD/JPY downside toward 150-152 seen as BoJ normalizes (hike expected next week, another in Q4/December).
- GBP/USD expected range-bound with bearish bias near 1.34; EUR/GBP offers upside potential.
- Elevated UST 10y yields near 5% and record short positioning are a key global risk-sentiment driver for EM rates and currencies broadly.

**Watch list**
- Tonight's August US CPI print — a soft reading is the main swing factor against a Fed hike.
- Next week's Fed decision and BoJ policy meeting.
- Oil prices and Gulf export/Iran tanker developments ahead of US midterm elections in November.
- ECB path toward a possible 25bp hike by December (deposit rate toward 2.75%).

episodes.title: Bessent's yen bet, cold Argentine data centers set, and the summer box office net
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly challenged FX markets to "bet against" the dollar's yen intervention stance, a notable signal given his hedge-fund history (including the 1990s $10bn bet against the British pound). The episode also covers a proposed $25bn OpenAI data center in Argentine Patagonia and record US/Canada summer box office revenue, both lower relevance for FX/rates but the Patagonia item touches Argentina's investment/FX narrative under President Javier Milei.

**Key points**
- USDJPY currently around 153.63.
- Japan's authorities have spent record amounts intervening to support the yen by purchasing it in FX markets.
- The US Treasury and Japan's finance ministry conducted a joint yen-buying intervention over the summer, the first coordinated action of this kind since 2011.
- Bessent's concern: Japan's finance ministry may need to sell US Treasury holdings to fund yen purchases, since Japan is a major foreign holder of US government debt.
- This follows a separate effort by Bessent to buy back Treasury bonds to push yields lower.
- Separately, OpenAI has signed a letter of intent to explore a $25bn data center in Patagonia, Argentina, partly for its naturally cold climate (cooling can account for ~40% of data center electricity use); Milei's government is courting AI investment with tax breaks and regulatory certainty.

**FX / rates implications**
- USDJPY: US Treasury rhetoric and coordinated FX intervention history signal Washington's tolerance limits on yen weakness — watch for further verbal or actual intervention risk that could trigger sharp JPY moves and spill into broader Asia FX positioning/carry trades.
- UST 10y: If Japan's MOF sells Treasuries to fund yen support, this is a bearish supply/price risk for USTs, pushing yields higher — a direct read-through to EM Asia rates and borrowing costs given UST yields anchor EM local rates.
- ARS/Argentina: Large-scale AI infrastructure investment interest is a modest positive data point for Argentina's FX/investment narrative under Milei's tax-break courtship strategy, though nothing concrete has broken ground yet.

**Watch list**
- Further Bessent statements or Treasury/BOJ coordinated intervention on JPY.
- Japan MOF Treasury holdings/sales data for signs of funding pressure.
- Progress (or lack thereof) on the OpenAI Patagonia data center as an Argentina investment signal.

episodes.title: Summer’s over, but what next for currency markets?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
NatWest's Brian Daingerfield and Paul Robson review end-of-summer macro themes: higher long-end global yields driven by fiscal stimulus expectations and elevated energy prices (Iran war stalemate stalling oil supply normalization), blurred Fed/Treasury reaction functions, UK fiscal risk ahead of the October 28 budget, and a sharp yen rally decoupling from oil prices.

**Key points**
- Fed's September decision (recorded Thursday, Sep 10) seen as a toss-up between a 25bp hike and hold, hinging on Friday's CPI print; Chair Powell's messaging has swung from hawkish (Jackson Hole) to mixed, with Waller and Williams more dovish.
- US Treasury's long-end buyback program came in above prior guidance but below market expectations, adding volatility/risk premium to USD assets.
- UK: front-end pricing near four 25bp BoE hikes over the coming year looks excessive versus NatWest's call of just two (November and February); sterling ranges near 25-year lows despite yield volatility; October 28 budget is the key fiscal catalyst.
- ECB kept a mildly hawkish tone on inflation persistence from oil, with further hikes seen as increasingly plausible; EUR/USD driven partly by German-Italian/French bond spreads and reviving European political risk (German election).
- USD/JPY fell roughly 10 big figures (164 to ~154) over six weeks without confirmed MOF/BOJ intervention, seen as a psychological break in yen-funding carry trades; BOJ expected to hike later in September; Japan pension fund reallocation toward local assets flagged as a longer-term yen support; Japan's planned consumption-tax cut (8% to 1% on food) raises fresh fiscal-funding skepticism.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising energy prices and long-end yield pressure raise global inflation/term-premium risk, a mild USD-supportive, broad risk-negative backdrop relevant to EM carry trades and EM local bond yields.
- Divergent central bank reaction functions (Fed ambiguity, BoE caution, ECB hawkish tilt, BOJ hike bias) argue for continued G10 rate-differential trading that also frames EM rate-differential/carry positioning.
- Yen's fundamental-versus-positioning driven rally reduces the attractiveness of yen as a funding currency for EM carry trades, a key input for EM FX carry strategies.

**Watch list**
- US CPI (Friday) and September FOMC decision.
- UK budget, October 28.
- BOJ meeting later in September for hike signal and hawkish guidance risk.
- Oil/energy prices tied to Iran war negotiations as a driver of global yields and inflation expectations.
- Japan pension fund asset-allocation flows into JGBs as a structural yen support signal.

episodes.title: Global Data Pod: The ECB is on the move, will the BoE follow?
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JP Morgan economists discuss how a sharp energy-price shock, driven by an intensifying Middle East crisis, has flipped the ECB and BoE narrative from growth fragility to resilient growth plus a serious inflation problem, sharply repricing hike expectations for both central banks. The ECB just met and laid out a hawkish staff forecast; the BoE decides next week with markets debating whether it should move even sooner.

**Key points**
- Markets now price 3+ ECB hikes over the next 9-12 months, with real debate over back-to-back hikes in October and December; ECB staff's baseline sees 2028 inflation at 2.3% (core 2.4%) even with 3+ hikes priced, and current energy spot/forward prices are closer to the ECB's hawkish adverse scenario.
- ECB headline inflation forecast to peak near 4%, staying elevated before easing; euro-area PMIs (July/August) have accelerated despite the Middle East crisis reintensifying over summer.
- UK: July GDP rose 0.4% m/m on top of a strong June; strength is broad-based (AI-related software/cloud investment, housing, employment) with the REC survey showing permanent placements at a 4-year high.
- UK CPI forecast to peak near 4% (possibly higher) in Q1 2027 due to delayed pass-through from the Ofgem price cap (+15% Jan, +9% April), staying between 3.5-4% into Q2; BoE's own analysis flags 3-4% as the threshold where inflation non-linearities/second-round wage effects become a concern.
- Analysts expect ECB to skip October and hike in December (risk skewed to more); BoE expected to hike in November rather than next week, mainly for communication/expectations-management reasons even though the data justifies a move now.

**FX / rates implications**
- Hawkish repricing of ECB and BoE tightening paths supports EUR and GBP against USD, with knock-on effects for DXY and broad risk sentiment relevant to EM carry trades.
- Sustained high energy (oil/gas) prices are a global inflation shock that could pressure EM central banks (India, Indonesia, Philippines, etc.) via imported inflation and terms-of-trade effects, especially energy importers.
- Higher UST/Bund/Gilt yield expectations as DM rate paths re-price higher raise the bar for EM local rates and could pressure EM FX carry if global yields rise faster than expected.

**Watch list**
- Bank of England meeting next week, plus UK CPI data due just before it, which could sway the decision.
- ECB October meeting: skip vs. back-to-back hike decision; December meeting with new staff forecasts.
- Middle East crisis trajectory — key swing factor for oil/gas prices and the peak of DM rate pricing.

episodes.title: The Week Ahead - Crunch time for the Fed and the BOJ
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A packed central-bank week: US August CPI just printed hot, cementing Nomura's call for a 25bp Fed hike next week; the ECB delivered an expected 25bp hike with hawkish forecast revisions; and the BOJ is set to hike 25bp next week amid a hawkish tone risk. Long-end global bond yields have hit multi-year highs and Brent crude keeps rising on the Middle East conflict, a common inflationary thread across all central banks.

**Key points**
- US CPI rose 0.3% m/m in August vs 0.22% expected; PPI and PCE-relevant components also came in hot, pointing to accelerating core PCE.
- Nomura now expects the Fed to hike 25bp next week and again in December, consistent with the dot plot; Chair Worsh likely to reiterate hawkish Jackson Hole rhetoric and flag oil-driven inflation risk.
- ECB hiked 25bp to a 2.5% deposit rate (top of its 1.75-2.50% neutral range), with upward GDP and HICP/core HICP revisions (including for 2028); Nomura pencils two more hikes (December, March).
- BOE expected to stay on hold through year-end then cut twice next year, a contrast to the ECB given UK rates already moderately restrictive; wage data due next week should support this.
- BOJ widely expected to hike 25bp next week; watch hawkish dissenter Takata (50bp proposal), reflationist dissent from Asada/Sato, and Governor Ueda's tone on the pace of future hikes, especially if the Fed hikes first (could push Ueda more hawkish to limit yen depreciation).
- China August data expected soft: retail sales +0.5% y/y, industrial production +4.7% y/y, fixed asset investment ~-11% y/y.
- Taiwan's CBC expected on hold but hawkish, with 2026 GDP forecast revised up to 11% y/y.
- India CPI expected to rise to 4.9% y/y in August (from 4.4%), core CPI up to 4.2% from 3.9%.

**FX / rates implications**
- Hawkish Fed hike plus hot CPI supports USD and pushes UST yields higher, a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades broadly.
- BOJ hike plus hawkish Ueda risk supportive of JPY; watch for October hike signaling.
- Rising Brent on Middle East conflict is a broad EM negative via import bills (esp. oil importers like India, Philippines, Thailand) but supportive for commodity exporters.
- Higher India CPI print raises pressure on RBI policy expectations; INR to watch amid inflation acceleration and elevated oil prices.
- ECB hawkish hike path (Dec/March) supports EUR; BOE divergence (on hold, cuts next year) is GBP-negative relative to EUR.

**Watch list**
- FOMC decision next week (25bp hike expected).
- BOJ policy meeting and Ueda press conference next week, plus Japan August CPI (Friday) and trade data (Wednesday).
- BOE meeting next week.
- China August activity data (retail sales, IP, FAI).
- Taiwan CBC meeting September 7 (hawkish hold expected).
- India August CPI print.
- New Zealand Q2 GDP.
- Brent crude trajectory amid ongoing Middle East conflict.

episodes.title: Global FX: Post-CPI and pre-Fed FX round up
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JPMorgan's G10 and EMFX strategists debate why the dollar hasn't rallied despite a hot CPI print, a hawkish Jackson Hole from Chair Warsh, and near-certain Fed hikes priced for next week's FOMC. The core discussion pivots to which currencies — DM and EM — are best insulated from a Fed hiking cycle, with a strong focus on carry as the key differentiator.

**Key points**
- Core CPI beat by a tick (0.29%); super-core hit 0.51%, the hottest since January, despite softer rent components.
- Fed hike next week is ~90% priced (22bp), with over three hikes priced further out; DXY has stopped tracking FOMC pricing, creating a valuation "chasm."
- JPM stays structurally dollar-bullish into FOMC but flags asymmetric downside risk if the Fed under-delivers on hawkishness even while hiking.
- BoE, BoJ and Fed all meet next week; JPM tactically constructive on GBP, USD and JPY into these meetings.
- GBI-EM FX total returns have stayed positive YTD despite the bond selloff — a resilience JPM calls surprising given weak US real yields, oil and copper backdrop.

**FX / rates implications**
- High-carry EM: COP, BRL seen as standard high-carry outperformers if the Fed reprices hawkishly; MXN also resilient on low positioning and strong BOP support despite modest carry.
- HUF flagged as an emerging resilient story as the central bank shows increasing sensitivity to FX weakness/gas-price beta.
- ZAR and CLP singled out as most vulnerable to further Fed repricing, but also highest-beta if the Fed surprises dovish.
- In DM, NOK and GBP most insulated from Fed hikes (high yielders), while CHF and SEK remain the preferred shorts/funders; EUR also favored as a funding currency given low relative carry and energy-price exposure.
- AUD flagged as a favored high-carry, terms-of-trade play alongside NOK versus low-yielding funders.

**Watch list**
- FOMC decision and tone next week — degree of hawkishness will determine whether DXY finally validates pricing.
- BoE and BoJ meetings same week — risk of disappointment if policy delivery doesn't match priced expectations.
- Energy prices (gas, oil) — key swing factor for EUR, NOK and HUF reaction functions.
- German state elections and Euro-area budget noise as medium-term EUR drags.

episodes.title: Hikes on the Horizon, Diesel Distress and Remembering September 11 9/11/26
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
A CNBC markets show centers on a sharply higher probability (85-86%) of a Fed rate hike next week, driven by sticky core CPI, weak consumer sentiment/inflation expectations, and a Middle East-driven oil shock pushing US diesel above $6/gallon for the first time. JPMorgan's chief US economist now expects two hikes this year (next week plus December), citing Fed credibility risk after Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole rhetoric, even as growth stays resilient.

**Key points**
- Core CPI came in firmer than expected; core PCE running near 3.3%, well above Fed target.
- 2-year UST yield hit multi-year highs (~462-465bp), about 100bp above the current Fed funds rate, which strategists read as evidence policy is too easy; 10-year yield near 4.95%.
- Preliminary September University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to near record lows; 1-year inflation expectations jumped to 4.6%, medium-term 3.4%.
- Iran-aligned Houthis seized Yemen's Parham island and struck Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline; Gulf states reportedly losing confidence in US security guarantees after Trump declined MBS's request to strike the Houthis.
- Oil (WTI) fell ~2.5% to about $100/barrel despite the escalation, partly on soft Chinese demand; strategists warn a further $5+ spike is possible if pipeline strikes continue and China/SPR demand returns.
- Wells Fargo CIO sees Fed credibility on the line: a hold next week could unwind, house view leans toward three hikes vs. consensus two; flags 10-year yield risk premium concerns above 5.25-5.5%.

**FX / rates implications**
- A confirmed Fed hike cycle (2-3 hikes into year-end) supports continued USD/DXY strength and higher UST yields, a headwind for EM Asia and LATAM carry trades and a driver of further EM currency depreciation pressure (INR, IDR, PHP, MXN, BRL all sensitive to US rate repricing).
- Elevated oil prices from Middle East supply risk (diesel at record highs) pressure oil-importing EM current accounts (India, Philippines, Indonesia) via terms-of-trade and inflation channels, while supporting oil exporters (Colombia, Mexico via Pemex-adjacent flows).
- Broad risk-on equity resilience despite rising yields suggests markets are not yet pricing full hawkish follow-through; a hawkish surprise next week could trigger a sharper EM FX selloff and UST curve repricing.

**Watch list**
- FOMC decision next week (CME FedWatch ~85-86% probability of a hike).
- December FOMC meeting for a potential second hike.
- Middle East escalation trajectory (Houthi attacks, Gulf-Iran talks Monday) and oil price reaction.
- 10-year UST yield levels near 5.25-5.5% flagged as a risk-premium inflection point.

episodes.title: How Global Finance Blocks Caribbean Climate Action
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Economist Marla Dukaran discusses how the global financial system structurally disadvantages Caribbean sovereigns facing climate disasters, using Jamaica's post-Hurricane Melissa recovery as a case study in disaster-resilient fiscal planning. The episode is a niche development-finance and sovereign-risk discussion with limited direct transmission to G10/EM Asia-LATAM FX and rates markets, but it touches on sovereign debt sustainability, credit ratings and multilateral financing mechanisms relevant to frontier/small-sovereign credit investors.

**Key points**
- Jamaica is the only Caribbean country expected to contract this year due to lingering Hurricane Melissa effects, but recovered strongly via CRIF (Caribbean climate catastrophe insurance fund, its biggest-ever payout), concessionary IMF credit lines, and multilateral bank support (CDB, IDB, CAF).
- Most Caribbean nations' FX reserves are effectively borrowed (some over 100% of reserves), a structural vulnerability layered on top of climate risk.
- Debt sustainability threshold cited at ~55% debt-to-GDP (per Barbados central bank governor Kevin Greenidge's research); Cayman Islands cited as a fiscally disciplined model (fiscal surplus, <10% debt/GDP).
- Catastrophe clauses in sovereign debt (pioneered by Grenada in 2015) allow repayment pauses after disasters; Dukaran is skeptical of the Bridgetown Initiative, viewing it as overly debt-reliant rather than insurance/grant-based.
- UN tax convention negotiations underway could reshape global tax governance and carve-outs for climate-vulnerable states.

**FX / rates implications**
- Minimal direct read-through for core EM Asia/LATAM FX or rates; relevant mainly to specialist Caribbean/frontier sovereign credit and catastrophe-bond investors.
- Broader theme of climate-driven credit rating downgrades raising borrowing costs is a generic risk factor for small, high-debt sovereigns rather than his core book.

**Watch list**
- UN global tax convention negotiations and potential climate-vulnerability carve-outs.
- Any Caribbean sovereign rating actions or catastrophe bond/insurance payouts following future hurricane seasons.

episodes.title: FX Moment: The Fed Meeting & What It Means for Bonds, the Dollar
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Bloomberg Intelligence's Audrey Child Freeman (Chief FX Strategist) and Ira Jersey (Chief US Rates Strategist) preview the September 16-17 FOMC meeting, recorded just after the US August CPI print. The market is pricing a 25bp hike as near-certain, with the dot plot and Chair Kevin Warsh's communication style the key swing factors for the dollar and Treasury curve.

**Key points**
- Market has priced roughly 75bp of hikes between now and mid-2026, split as a hike now, one in January, and another around May-September 2026.
- A hold (no hike) would be a major surprise and a Fed credibility shock, given repeated market-guidance signaling.
- 10-year UST has a key resistance/cycle-high level at 5.02%; 30-year yields have already been making new highs and could extend further on a hold.
- This is the last dot plot with a 2026 median forecast before Warsh's tenure fully takes over messaging; 2027 dots will get outsized market attention.
- One-year inflation swaps have risen from ~2% to 2.6% for next August, showing the market doesn't see inflation reliably at the 2% target even after the base-effect decline expected by mid-2026.
- Warsh's four prior public appearances (two press conferences, semiannual testimony, Jackson Hole) have all been read as hawkish.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed hold would be dollar-negative on both cyclical/yield and structural/credibility grounds, especially with G10 peers (e.g., SNB this week) still signaling more tightening — this favors EM Asia and LATAM carry currencies broadly.
- A hike alone won't spark a durable dollar rally; needs accompanying hawkish guidance (keeping a further-hike option open) to sustain USD strength against EM.
- A hold scenario risks bear-steepening/twist-steepening of the UST curve, which would pressure EM local rates via higher US long-end yields and could widen EM spreads.

**Watch list**
- FOMC decision and dot plot, September 16-17.
- 10-year UST resistance at 5.02% (prior cycle high).
- Chair Warsh's press conference tone/reaction function guidance.
- BoJ policy meeting, following closely after the Fed.
